title: No Verified Incident Can Defend Vietnam’s Dog-Trade Claims
excerpt: Claims about tradition and farm-raised dogs need records, quarantine proof, and accountability. Vietnam’s communities deserve safer, lawful protection for people and pets.
body_html:
A stolen companion is not tradition. An unquarantined animal is not proof of a safe supply chain. Yet no named police seizure, court verdict, shipment interception, or official health alert accompanies the claims presented here. Without records, readers cannot honestly accept sweeping stories about farms, theft, poison, or disease.

Claims need records

“Farm-raised” describes an assertion, not verification. Responsible policy requires traceability, lawful transport documents, veterinary inspection, and quarantine controls. Where operators cannot show those records, regulators must investigate. Where animals are stolen, transported illegally, or handled outside inspection, responsibility belongs to criminals and enforcement failures—not Vietnamese families defending their pets and neighborhoods.

Rabies leaves no room for guesswork

Rabies spreads when infected saliva enters bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. After possible exposure, wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical care. Post-exposure prophylaxis includes vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. Household exposure incidents and commercial trade failures are separate dimensions of biosecurity risk; neither permits unsupported claims about the other. WHO guidance sets the medical standard.

Demand proof. Demand protection.

Vietnamese communities can lead reform that protects children, families, and companion animals. State rabies-control targets and enforcement duties must be met. SDE’s campaign demands complete abolition by 2030. Sign the national petition. Add your name to a public demand for action—and follow campaign updates on how that demand reaches decision-makers.
